titre: The Cyrus Cylinder: An Inscription for Marduk, Not a Charter of Rights
accroche: Presented in 1971 as the first declaration of human rights, the Cyrus Cylinder is a Babylonian foundation inscription.
contenu_vulgarise:
A baked-clay cylinder about twenty-two centimeters long, covered in tight cuneiform signs: at the British Museum, it is displayed under the label “Cyrus Cylinder.” It is often presented as the first charter of human rights, and a replica of it was given to the United Nations. What the text says is narrower, and more religious.

## A Foundation Deposit

Hormuzd Rassam, an archaeologist working for the British Museum, discovered the cylinder in March 1879 in Babylon, on the site of the temple of Esagila. It dates from the years following Cyrus's capture of the city in 539 BCE. Written in Akkadian, in about forty-five lines, it is a foundation inscription: the kind of text that the kings of Mesopotamia buried in the walls of a building they had just rebuilt, so that the gods and their successors would know who had done it and why.

The account follows an ancient pattern. The previous king, Nabonidus, made “the worship of Marduk, the king of the gods” cease and “did evil continually against the city of Marduk.” Marduk, angered, looks for a just king; he takes as his favorite a man whose name he pronounces: Cyrus. The conqueror then presents himself as a restorer: he returns to the sanctuaries the images of the gods who had resided there, gathers the inhabitants, and returns their dwellings to them.

## What the Kings of Mesopotamia Said of Themselves

These gestures were read, in 1971, as proof of an unprecedented tolerance. The Shah of Iran made the cylinder the centerpiece of the festivities celebrating 2,500 years of the Persian monarchy, and presented it as a founding text of human rights. Specialists dispute this reading as anachronistic: the text belongs to the tradition of Babylonian and Assyrian builders' inscriptions. Its function is to legitimize the king, who says he was chosen by the god of the city he has just taken, and not to proclaim rights.

The cylinder is also invoked in connection with the return of the Jews from Babylon, which the Book of Ezra attributes to Cyrus. The text itself mentions only Mesopotamian sanctuaries; it names neither Jerusalem nor Judea.

The shift: an object cited to support modern values becomes more interesting when read for itself. It shows a conqueror who wins a city by making himself the servant of its god: a religious policy before it is a morality. What does a text tell us about the era in which it is found, when we are not looking in it for what we wanted to read there?

repere.texte: The Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum, BM 90920) was found in March 1879 in Babylon by Hormuzd Rassam. Written in Akkadian in about 45 lines, it accuses Nabonidus of having made “the worship of Marduk” cease and says of Cyrus: “I gathered all their inhabitants and returned their dwellings to them” (trans. Cogan, after Livius.org).
repere.source: Translation by Mordechai Cogan (The Context of Scripture, vol. II, 2003), adapted to Schaudig's edition, lines 7, 8, 12, and 31-32

carte.punch: The Cyrus Cylinder is not a charter of human rights: it is a text for Marduk.
carte.idee: Discovered in Babylon in 1879, the Cyrus Cylinder (c. 539 BCE) is a foundation inscription: in it, Cyrus returns their gods to the sanctuaries and says he was chosen by Marduk. Specialists consider it anachronistic to read a declaration of rights into it.
carte.source_courte: Cogan, trans. of the Cyrus Cylinder, 2003

quiz.question: What type of text is the Cyrus Cylinder, according to specialists?
choix: A peace treaty signed with the kings of subject peoples
A penal law applied across the whole Persian empire
A Babylonian foundation inscription that legitimizes the king before the gods
A manifesto of religious tolerance written for all the peoples of the empire
quiz.explication: It is a builder's inscription in the Babylonian and Assyrian tradition, which presents Cyrus as chosen by Marduk. It is neither a treaty, nor a penal code, nor a manifesto of tolerance: reading the text as a manifesto is the anachronistic reading that specialists dispute.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Cyrus do, according to the text of the cylinder, after taking Babylon?
choix: He imposes the worship of Marduk on all the peoples of the Persian empire
He returns the images of the gods to the sanctuaries and their dwellings to the inhabitants
He has the temple of Jerusalem rebuilt on Marduk's orders
He abolishes the worship of Marduk in favor of a single Persian god
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that Cyrus returns to the sanctuaries the images of the gods who resided there and gathers the inhabitants to return their dwellings to them; it mentions neither Jerusalem, nor the imposition of a cult, nor the abolition of Marduk's.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do specialists judge the presentation of the cylinder as a charter of human rights, made in 1971 by the Shah of Iran?
choix: Faithful to the text, which already uses the word “right”
Partially accurate, only for the return of the Jews from Babylon
Anachronistic, the text belonging to the genre of Babylonian foundation inscriptions
Since confirmed by the discovery of a second, identical cylinder
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Specialists judge this reading anachronistic: the text belongs to the tradition of Babylonian and Assyrian foundation inscriptions, which legitimize the king before the gods, and mentions neither rights nor the return of the Jews from Babylon.
